title: Unipolarity, American Hegemony and Multipolarity

cards.b:
This is the most live question in IR. After the Soviet Union fell in 1991, the US stood alone. Three decades later, China is a peer rival, Russia has gone to war in Europe, and many middle powers act on their own. What kind of order is this?

The syllabus title links three ideas: unipolarity (one dominant power), American hegemony (a dominant power that also leads through rules and institutions) and multipolarity (several centres of power).

UPSC asks about this theme in many forms: "Is the world multipolar?", "Has American hegemony ended?", "India's place in a multipolar world". It also feeds into Paper II Section B on India-US, India-China and India-Russia relations.

This topic changes every year, so learn the concepts and the thinkers, then update with two or three recent facts (tariffs, the war in West Asia, BRICS). Always put the date next to a fact.

Polarity counts the great powers that shape the system, judged by their share of military, economic, technological and diplomatic power. Waltz made polarity the main variable in Theory of International Politics (1979).

  • Unipolar: one power far ahead of the rest.
  • Bipolar: two superpowers (1945-91).
  • Multipolar: three or more major powers.

A related word, hegemony, means leadership with consent as well as power. Charles Kindleberger and Robert Gilpin argued that an open world economy needs a hegemon to supply public goods. This is hegemonic stability theory.

Debate over stability: Waltz thought bipolarity safest, Deutsch and Singer (1964) argued multipolarity is safer, and Wohlforth (1999) said unipolarity is peaceful.

Charles Krauthammer's essay "The Unipolar Moment" (Foreign Affairs, winter 1990-91) claimed that the US stood alone at the top. He thought the moment might be brief.

Key events:

  • 1991 Gulf War. A US-led coalition, authorised by the UN Security Council, expelled Iraq from Kuwait. Bush spoke of a "new world order".
  • 1990s. Interventions in Somalia (1993), Bosnia (1995) and Kosovo (1999, NATO without UN approval). NATO expanded to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic in 1999.
  • Economic lead. US-led institutions (IMF, World Bank, WTO) set the rules. Washington Consensus ideas spread.
  • Idea of "end of history" (Fukuyama): liberal democracy had no rival.

William Wohlforth, in "The Stability of a Unipolar World" (International Security, 1999), argued that the US lead was so large that no rival could challenge it, so the system was peaceful and durable.

Hard power

Unmatched military reach, with hundreds of overseas bases, aircraft carriers and a nuclear triad. SIPRI estimates US military spending in 2024 at nearly $1 trillion, over three times China's estimated figure.

Economic power

The largest economy for decades (about a quarter of world GDP in nominal terms), and the dollar as the main reserve and trade currency, which gives the US financial sanctions power. Top universities and technology firms.

Soft power

Joseph Nye, Bound to Lead (1990) and Soft Power (2004): attraction through culture, values and institutions.

Institutions and alliances

G. John Ikenberry, After Victory (2001) and Liberal Leviathan (2011), argued the US built a rules-based liberal international order that others joined because it was open and constrained US power. NATO and alliances in Asia anchored it.

The attacks of 11 September 2001 changed US strategy.

  • War in Afghanistan (2001) and the invasion of Iraq (2003) without a clear UN mandate. The 2002 National Security Strategy embraced pre-emption.
  • The costs: trillions of dollars, loss of lives, and damage to legitimacy as no weapons of mass destruction were found.
  • Chaos in Iraq, the rise of ISIS (2014), and the chaotic US exit from Afghanistan (August 2021).

The 2008 global financial crisis, which began in the US, hurt the image of the US economic model. The G20 leaders' summit (first held in 2008) recognised that emerging economies had to be at the table.

Scholars like Paul Kennedy (The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers, 1987) warned about "imperial overstretch". Chalmers Johnson (Blowback, 2000) and others made a similar point on empire's costs.

Fareed Zakaria, The Post-American World (2008), described the "rise of the rest": the US is not declining in absolute terms, but others are catching up. Richard Haass called it "nonpolarity" (2008): power is spread among states, firms, NGOs and militias. Amitav Acharya, The End of American World Order (2014), spoke of a "multiplex world".

  • China. From the 2001 WTO entry to the world's second-largest economy. The Belt and Road Initiative (2013), the AIIB (opened 2016) and a modern navy.
  • Russia. Crimea (2014) and the invasion of Ukraine (February 2022). Closer ties with China and North Korea.
  • BRICS (2009), expanded in 2024 with Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE, and Indonesia from 2025. The New Development Bank started in 2015.
  • Middle powers: India, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, Indonesia. They hedge and bargain.
  • EU as an economic and regulatory power.

Still unipolar?

Stephen Brooks and William Wohlforth, World Out of Balance (2008) and later work: the US still leads in military technology, finance, alliances and universities. No other state has the full set.

Bipolar (US-China)?

China and the US are far ahead of all others in GDP, technology and defence spending. Yan Xuetong of Tsinghua and others see a coming bipolar competition. John Mearsheimer says China's rise makes rivalry nearly certain.

Multipolar?

Russia, India, EU, Japan and regional powers shape outcomes. Military power is concentrated in two, but economic and diplomatic power is spread.

Disorder?

Ian Bremmer's "G-Zero" (2012): no one leads. Some say we have a "multipolar world without multilateralism".

Mearsheimer's view in "Bound to Fail" (International Security, 2019) is that the US-led liberal order was bound to fade, and a realist order, bounded by great-power balance, replaces it.

• US trade shock. Heavy tariffs from April 2025, challenged in court. On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that the emergency law (IEEPA) did not authorise tariffs. The administration used other laws, such as Section 122 (a temporary 150-day tariff that lapsed in July 2026) and then Section 301 tariffs on dozens of economies.
  • Retreat from institutions. The US left the Paris Agreement (effective January 2026) and WHO, and announced exits from dozens of other bodies in January 2026.
  • War in West Asia. US and Israeli strikes on Iran began again on 28 February 2026. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted. Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May 2026.
  • US-China. A trade truce was struck in October 2025 and talks continue.
  • Others. The Ukraine war continues. BRICS and the SCO have drawn more attention. India chaired BRICS in 2026.

These show a system with a still-powerful but less predictable US, a rival China, and wider room for middle powers. Treat each fact as of 2026, and re-check before the exam.

• India's preference. New Delhi has long said it wants a multipolar world, and a multipolar Asia too. Joint statements with Russia and France use this phrase.
  • Strategic autonomy and multi-alignment. India works with the US (Quad, defence and technology), Russia (energy and arms), France, Japan, Gulf states and the Global South.
  • Pressure test. In 2025 the US imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Indian goods, citing India's Russian oil purchases. India diversified: FTAs with the UK (in force 15 July 2026), the EU (concluded January 2026), and a US interim framework in February 2026. Rates and status are still evolving.
  • China. Improved tone in 2025 (Modi's visit to the SCO summit in Tianjin, August-September 2025), but border and trade issues remain.
  • Platforms. BRICS chair in 2026; G20 presidency in 2023; Voice of Global South summits; Quad; I2U2; IMEC (announced 2023).
  • Risk. Overreliance on one partner, and a gap between aspiration and capability. India's GDP is large, but per capita income and manufacturing remain low.

"The unipolar moment is over. Do you agree?"
"Is the world moving towards a multipolar order? What does this mean for India?"
"Examine the challenges to American hegemony."
"Compare the stability of bipolar and multipolar systems."

Structure: define polarity and hegemony (Waltz, Kindleberger, Gilpin). Show the unipolar moment (Krauthammer 1990-91, Wohlforth 1999). Sources of US power and Ikenberry's liberal order. Overreach (Iraq 2003, 2008 crisis). Rise of China, Russia and BRICS (Zakaria, Acharya). Debate: unipolar, bipolar, multipolar. Recent shocks, with dates. End with India: strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and a call for a reformed multilateral order.

Say what you think: "multipolar in economics, bipolar in military power, and increasingly disordered".

quiz.w: Krauthammer's essay appeared in Foreign Affairs.

quiz.q: William Wohlforth's 1999 article argued that unipolarity is:
quiz.w: 'The Stability of a Unipolar World' (International Security).

quiz.q: Hegemonic stability theory is associated with:
quiz.w: A hegemon supplies public goods for an open world economy.

quiz.q: G. John Ikenberry's Liberal Leviathan (2011) is about:
quiz.w: He argued that the US built a rules-based order that others joined.

quiz.q: Paul Kennedy's The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers (1987) warned about:
quiz.w: Great powers decline when commitments outrun economic strength.

quiz.q: BRICS expanded in January 2024 to include:
o: Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE
Argentina, Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh and Kenya

quiz.q: In February 2026, the US Supreme Court held in Learning Resources v. Trump that:
o: The WTO may review US tariffs
IEEPA does not authorise presidential tariffs

quiz.q: India's 2023 G20 presidency ended with the African Union becoming:
quiz.w: The AU became a permanent G20 member at the New Delhi summit.

quiz.q: Which book by Amitav Acharya describes a 'multiplex world'?
o: The End of American World Order (2014)
quiz.w: Acharya argued that the future order has many actors and no single leader.
